script.opening: “Hello. Another phone call about my bloods. Just tell me straight, doctor. And before you start, I’m not having an operation, whatever it is.”

facts.text: Confirms name and date of birth. At home on his own, happy to talk.

Tired for months, thirsty, up once or twice at night to wee, constipated, aching in his back and legs, “foggy”, forgetting things. Low and not enjoying much since Grace died. No vomiting, no confusion that others have noticed, no abdominal pain, no bone fractures. Weight steady.
Kidney stone two years ago: severe left loin pain, A&E, passed the stone, no follow-up. Hypertension for ten years.
Bendroflumethiazide and amlodipine. No lithium, no calcium or vitamin D supplements, no antacids. Drinks little water: “tea, mostly”.
Grace went in for a “routine” bowel operation and died of sepsis a week later. “They said it was routine. I watched her die.” He has decided he will never have surgery.
Lonely, low most days, sleeps badly. Sees his daughter at weekends. No thoughts of ending his life: “Grace wouldn’t want that.”

Courteous but guarded. Firm “no” to surgery. Softens if the doctor asks why, listens to his story about Grace, and does not push. Agrees to see the specialist “just to listen” and to the medicine changes.

ice.ideas: “It’s probably my age, or the grief making me tired.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA: his wife died after a ‘routine’ operation; he is terrified of surgery and of being pressured into it. Also feels foggy and worries it is dementia.
ice.expectations: “Tell me what it is, give me a tablet if there is one, and leave it at that.”

worked.txt: “Before I go through them, what have you been told about these blood tests so far?”

“Your calcium is a bit high on two tests, and the hormone that controls calcium, called PTH, is high too. That usually means one of four tiny glands in your neck, the parathyroids, has become overactive. It’s common, and it isn’t cancer.”
“You said you won’t have an operation before I’d mentioned one. Would you tell me what’s behind that?”
“I’m so sorry about Grace. After that, it makes complete sense that the word ‘operation’ feels terrifying. Nobody will make you have one.”

“Your calcium level and the kidney stone two years ago mean the national guidance recommends you see a specialist. Seeing them doesn’t commit you to anything; they’ll explain the choices, including not operating.”
“One of your blood pressure tablets can raise calcium, so I’ll swap it. Your vitamin D is low, so I’ll replace it. And plenty of water, not just tea.”

f.learning: Primary hyperparathyroidism is the commonest cause of hypercalcaemia in primary care: a raised albumin-adjusted calcium with a PTH that is raised or inappropriately normal. NICE NG132 (2019) advises measuring PTH when adjusted calcium is 2.6 mmol/L or above on two occasions (or 2.5 or above with suspected primary hyperparathyroidism), and not excluding the diagnosis if PTH is in the upper half of the normal range. Refer people with confirmed primary hyperparathyroidism to a specialist with expertise in parathyroid surgery if they have symptoms, end-organ disease (renal stones, fragility fractures or osteoporosis), or an albumin-adjusted calcium of 2.85 mmol/L or above. Parathyroidectomy is the only cure and has a high success rate; the specialist will exclude familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia (urine calcium), arrange imaging and assess bone density. For people who decline or are unsuitable for surgery, monitoring and, in some circumstances, cinacalcet are options. In primary care: review drugs (thiazides reduce urinary calcium excretion; lithium causes hyperparathyroidism; stop calcium and vitamin D supplements unless deficient), measure vitamin D and replace deficiency, advise good hydration, and do not restrict dietary calcium. Safety-net for severe hypercalcaemia (vomiting, confusion, abdominal pain, dehydration), which needs same-day care. Symptoms such as tiredness, thirst, constipation, aches, low mood and poor concentration may be due to hypercalcaemia and can be mistaken for grief or ageing. The communication skill is exploring a pre-emptive refusal: understanding the bereavement behind it, giving honest information, respecting autonomy, and agreeing a step he can accept, such as hearing the specialist’s options.

model.text: Hello, is that Mr Okoro? I’m Dr Clarke from the surgery. Could you confirm your date of birth? Is now a good time, and are you somewhere private?
Yes, it’s me, I’m on my own. Another phone call about my bloods. Just tell me straight, doctor. And before you start, I’m not having an operation, whatever it is.
I will be straight with you. I also heard what you said about an operation, and I’d like to come back to that. First, what have you been told about these tests so far?
Just that the calcium was up and they wanted another one.

That’s right. Your calcium is slightly high on both tests, and the hormone that controls calcium, called PTH, is high too. That usually means one of four tiny glands in your neck, the parathyroid glands, has become overactive. It’s common, and it isn’t cancer.
Well, that’s something.
Have you been feeling thirsty, weeing more, constipated, achy, or foggy in your thinking?
All of that, now you say it. I thought it was grief. I’ve been worried I’m going senile, to be honest.
Raised calcium can cause exactly that fogginess, and it can improve when the calcium is treated. Any vomiting, confusion, bad tummy pain? Have you had kidney stones or broken bones?
No sickness. I had a kidney stone two years ago. Agony. They never said anything about calcium.
Which tablets do you take? Any calcium or vitamin D, indigestion remedies, or lithium?
Just my two blood pressure tablets. Bendro-something and amlodipine.
Thank you. Can I ask what’s behind saying no to an operation before I’d mentioned one?
(pause) My wife, Grace. Three years ago. A routine bowel operation, they said. She got an infection and died a week later. I watched her die. I’m not going through that.
I’m so sorry. After that, the word ‘operation’ must feel terrifying. I want to be clear: nobody will make you have one. It’s your decision.
Thank you. Nobody’s said that.
How have you been in yourself since Grace died? Your mood, sleep, whether you’ve had thoughts of not wanting to go on?
Lonely. Low. I see my daughter at weekends. I’d never do anything, Grace wouldn’t want that.

Here’s what I’d suggest. Because your calcium is above a certain level and you’ve had a kidney stone, the national guidance says you should see a specialist in these glands. Seeing them doesn’t commit you to anything. They’ll do more tests and explain the choices, including not operating and keeping an eye on it, or tablets in some cases.
Just to listen?

Just to listen. If you wanted to know, the operation is usually through a small cut in the neck, often with a short hospital stay, and it’s very different from bowel surgery. But that’s for you and them to talk through.

There are things we can do now. Bendroflumethiazide can push calcium up, so I’ll stop it and start a different blood pressure tablet, and ask the nurse to check your pressure in two weeks. Your vitamin D is low, so I’ll prescribe a supplement. Drink plenty of water through the day, not just tea, and don’t cut out calcium in your food.
model.why: Thiazide switch; vitamin D; fluids; no dietary restriction

model.text: And with how low you’ve been, would you like some support? There’s bereavement counselling locally, and I’d like to see how you’re doing once the calcium is sorted.
I might. Yes.
Could you tell me what you’ll do from today?
Stop the bendro, start the new one. Vitamin D. Drink water. See the specialist just to hear them out. Bloods again.
Exactly. Repeat bloods in about four weeks. If you start vomiting, become confused or very drowsy, get bad tummy or loin pain, or can’t keep fluids down, call 111 or go to A&E the same day.
